clue.text: Sports official ordered inn meals

indicators.note: ordered says the letters of the words that follow are arranged into a new sequence

explanation.surface: A referee's assistant puts in an order for food at a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' looks like the official placing a food order, but it is the anagram signal on INN MEALS.
explanation.definitionFit: The touch judge who flags when the ball goes out of play is a sports official of this kind.

clue.text: Porky about repast ultimately with few calories?

indicators.note: about means the fib goes round the following letter

parts.note: porky is short for pork pie, rhyming slang for a lie

indicators.note: ultimately picks the final letter of the word repast

explanation.surface: A fib told about a meal claiming it was low in calories.
explanation.walkthrough: PORKY is British rhyming slang: pork pie = lie. The final T of 'repast' sits inside LIE.
explanation.definitionFit: A commercial spelling used on food and drink labels to mean low in fat or energy.

clue.text: Bomb from this country in North East

indicators.note: in means the country's letters go inside the compass direction

parts.note: NE is the compass abbreviation for north-east
for a British newspaper, this country is the UK

explanation.surface: A bomb comes from Britain, in the north-east of England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this country' means the UK because the setter writes for a British paper.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, it means to attack with atomic weapons, so to bomb.

clue.text: Small wait? I'd sounded naively idealistic

parts.note: to tarry is to linger or wait

indicators.note: sounded says the word before it is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: the contraction for I had, said out loud

explanation.surface: Someone who says they made only a short wait speaks with innocent optimism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sounded' says I'D is spoken, giving EYED.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreamily optimistic and unrealistic, as if dazzled by stars.

clue.text: Highest position of a Personnel Officer — that's surprising!

parts.note: PO is an abbreviation for personnel officer
gee is an exclamation of surprise

explanation.surface: Someone is amazed at how high a personnel officer has climbed.
explanation.definitionFit: The point in an orbit farthest from Earth, hence figuratively the peak or climax.

clue.text: Quarter of pint good? Bad!

parts.note: ill can mean bad, as in ill effects or ill will

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a quarter-pint measure is good, and answers that it is bad.
explanation.walkthrough: A gill is an old British liquid measure, a quarter of a pint.
explanation.definitionFit: An imperial measure of liquid equal to a quarter of a pint, five fluid ounces.

clue.text: Terrible rag I find beneath me?

indicators.note: terrible says the letters of the words after it are badly mangled

explanation.surface: Someone finds a dreadful rag beneath them, unworthy of their notice.
explanation.definitionFit: A Latin-derived phrase for what is below one's dignity or unbecoming.

clue.text: Awfully silly to a true friend?

indicators.note: awfully says the letters of the words after it are scrambled badly

explanation.surface: Someone behaves very foolishly towards a faithful companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awfully' looks like an intensifier for 'silly', but it is the anagram signal on SILLY TO A.
explanation.definitionFit: A faithful supporter of a cause or ruler, by extension a steadfast ally.

clue.text: Weak boat repaired? You did well!

indicators.note: repaired says the letters of the words before it are put back together in a different order

explanation.surface: Someone who fixed a leaky boat is congratulated on the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repaired' signals rearranging the letters of WEAK BOAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Telling someone to accept applause is a way of saying they deserve praise for their performance.

clue.text: Dubious judge initially leaves short time

indicators.note: leaves means the letter goes away from the word for a short time

parts.note: a jiffy is a moment, a short time

indicators.note: initially picks the opening letter of the word judge

explanation.surface: A doubtful judge walks out after a brief spell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' looks like the noun (pages), but it is a verb: the J from 'judge initially' departs from JIFFY.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally, something questionable or of uncertain quality is described with this word.

clue.text: Europeans going over a role having divergent views

parts.note: Poles are people from Poland, Europeans
a part is a role in a play

explanation.surface: Some Europeans rehearse a role while disagreeing completely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going over' joins the pieces, suggesting Poles reading through a role.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiomatically, two parties this far separated hold utterly opposed opinions.

clue.text: Brawl costing no one anything

definitions.meaning: a chaotic fight in which everyone joins in

explanation.surface: A fight breaks out, and at least nobody had to pay for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names both a general melee and something given away to everybody at no charge.

clue.text: Piece ragmen wrapped in paper

indicators.note: wrapped in means the word ragmen is placed inside the newspaper's letters

parts.note: the FT is the Financial Times, a newspaper
taken as written

explanation.surface: Rag-and-bone men get a piece wrapped up in newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The FT is the Financial Times, a British newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A broken-off part or small bit of something larger.

clue.text: A right fool, taken in by her tormenter

indicators.note: taken in by means the preceding letters go inside the word her

parts.note: taken as written
an ass is a fool

explanation.surface: A foolish man is deceived by the woman who torments him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken in by' reads as being fooled by her, but it is the containment signal: the fool ends up physically inside the woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who pesters or persistently bothers another person torments them.

clue.text: Back, having secured extremely portable farm machine

indicators.note: having secured means the back holds the following letters inside it

parts.note: the rear is the back of something

indicators.note: extremely picks the two letters at the ends of the word portable

explanation.surface: A portable farm machine has something fixed onto its back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' takes the end letters of 'portable'; 'having secured' says the back holds them.
explanation.definitionFit: A harvesting machine that cuts grain crops is named for the person who cuts them.

clue.text: Negligent about girl

parts.note: re means about or concerning, as in a letter's heading
a miss is a girl or young woman

explanation.surface: Someone is careless where a young woman is concerned.
explanation.definitionFit: Failing in one's duty and being careless are exact synonyms here.

clue.text: Father and mother embracing the Spanish girl

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father

indicators.note: embracing means the mother's letters hug the Spanish word

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother
el is the Spanish for the

explanation.surface: Parents hug the Spanish girl.
explanation.definitionFit: A female given name, so a girl in crossword terms.

clue.text: Central American met a month back with Alan

indicators.note: back means the words before it are written from right to left

parts.note: taken as written
Aug is the short form of August, a month
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man from Central America met someone a month ago, together with Alan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reads like 'ago' but turns round both 'met' and the month's short form; 'with' joins on the name.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of a country in Central America bordering Mexico, whose capital shares its name.

clue.text: Loathsome guy too hard on regular basis

indicators.note: on regular basis picks every other letter, starting from the first, of the words too hard

explanation.surface: A nasty man is routinely far too harsh.
explanation.definitionFit: An amphibian name used figuratively for a repulsive or contemptible person.

clue.text: Ancient city's weight system for metals

definitions.meaning: the city of Homer's Iliad, besieged by the Greeks
the system of weights used for precious metals and gems

explanation.surface: An old city is the source of a way of weighing metals.
explanation.definitionFit: The same word names Homer's besieged city and the ounce system for gold and silver.

clue.text: Part of hotel seems different

indicators.note: Part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Some of the hotel appears to have changed.
explanation.definitionFit: Used after a pronoun, as in someone or something other, it means different or another.

clue.text: Severely criticize a rule Bob concocted

indicators.note: concocted says the letters of the words before it are made up into something new

explanation.surface: Bob invented a rule and is roundly attacked for it.
explanation.definitionFit: To attack verbally at length, or argue a point excessively, is the sense here.

clue.text: Flag that is reluctantly exhibited first of all

indicators.note: first of all picks the opening letter of each of the four words that follow

explanation.surface: A flag, it seems, was put on show only grudgingly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flag' looks like a banner, but here it is the verb meaning to weaken.
explanation.definitionFit: To flag is to grow weary or lose energy, the same as becoming fatigued.

clue.text: Daughter agreed toy ad changes as routine

parts.note: ay (aye) is an old word of agreement, yes

indicators.note: changes says the letters of the words after it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A daughter consents as a toy advert gets altered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changes' rearranges TOY AD to give TODAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordinary and everyday, as in the regular running of a business.
